visits.text: Arrive in Amphawa in early afternoon. The floating market comes alive from 2 PM but reveals its true character from 5 PM onward, when lamps illuminate the canal's wooden houses. Cooking boats offer pad thai, grilled prawns, mango sticky rice from the water. You order from the quay, boats dock to deliver.

By boat, reach Wat Bang Kung - an 18th-century military temple whose main hall is literally consumed by the roots of a giant banyan tree. The roots have invaded the walls for two centuries, encircling Buddhas and columns in an embrace of stone and wood.

activities.text: After 8 PM, board a nighttime boat ride on the Mae Klong River to observe fireflies. Hundreds of insects synchronize to flash together in trees along the banks - a rare natural phenomenon. The ride lasts about one hour.

visits.text: Take the train from Bangkok (departure from Hua Lamphong or Krung Thep Aphiwat, approximately 90 minutes). Upon arriving in Ayutthaya, rent a bicycle - it's the best way to navigate between ruins. Begin with Wat Mahathat, founded in 1374. It's world-famous for its Buddha head - decapitated during the 1767 Burmese invasion - that became trapped in the roots of a bodhi tree. Legend says the tree caught and cradled it as it rolled there. You kneel to photograph it.

Cross the square to Wat Phra Si Sanphet. This was the kingdom's largest temple, reserved for royal use exclusively. Its three bell-shaped chedis, dating from the 15th and 16th centuries, house the ashes of three Ayutthaya sovereigns. At its peak, a 52-foot gilded Buddha statue stood here - it was melted down by the Burmese in 1767 to recover its 756 pounds of gold.

Just beside it, enter Wihan Phra Mongkhon Bophit - a still-active temple housing one of the country's largest bronze Buddha statues, standing 40.8 feet tall. Unlike neighboring ruins, this temple breathes with life: monks meditate here, incense burns, jasmine flowers are offered.

Rise before 6:30 AM and cycle toward Wat Chaiwatthanaram on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River. Built in 1630 by King Prasat Thong, this Khmer-style temple aligns a 115-foot central prang surrounded by eight chedis connected by a gallery of Buddhas - nearly all decapitated. At sunrise, the golden raking light on the laterite silhouettes creates one of Ayutthaya's most striking images.

Late morning, head to Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon outside the center. Its main chedi rises 236 feet, dominating the plain. Around it, some fifty seated Buddhas wrapped in saffron cloth form an impressive row. This is one of Ayutthaya's best-preserved temples and a powerful image of Thai devotion.

activities.text: In the afternoon, explore Ayutthaya island by bicycle. The archaeological site spans 714 acres surrounded by three rivers. Pedal between isolated prangs, decapitated Buddhas aligned along galleries, lichen-covered stupas. Wat Ratchaburana warrants a stop: climb into the prang and descend into the underground crypt where 15th-century frescoes survived.

In the afternoon, take time to wander Ayutthaya Floating Market (east of the island). It's more recent than traditional markets but offers a fine showcase of local cuisine: boat noodles (kuay tiao reua), khao mok kai (Thai version of biryani), and giant river prawns. Order from the quays.

visits.text: Enter the Grand Palace through the Mani Noppharat Gate (new entrance since January 2024). This 54-acre complex houses Wat Phra Kaew and its Emerald Buddha - a 24-inch jade sculpture draped in gold whose robes the king himself changes three times a year according to the season. Interior galleries unfold murals of the Ramakien, the Thai version of the Ramayana, across nearly a mile of walls. Allow at least 2 hours. Cover shoulders and legs.

Exit the Grand Palace and walk 10 minutes to Wat Pho. Step into the main chapel: the Reclining Buddha stretches 151 feet long and 49 feet high, entirely covered in gold leaf. His feet are inlaid with mother-of-pearl depicting the 108 auspicious characteristics of Buddha. The temple has also housed since 1962 the Thai massage school that has trained over 200,000 practitioners.

Take the ferry from Tha Tien pier (4 baht) to cross the Chao Phraya. On the opposite bank, Wat Arun reveals itself: its central prang tower rises 269 feet, encrusted with colored porcelain fragments once donated by Bangkok residents. Climb the steep steps for the river view. Late afternoon, the light sets the mosaics ablaze - it's the best time to visit.

Push open the door to Jim Thompson's House in the Siam district. This American, a former OSS agent, reconstructed six traditional teak houses purchased from Ayutthaya, then assembled them here in 1959 along a canal. He filled them with a collection of Thai, Burmese, and Cambodian Buddhist art before mysteriously vanishing in Malaysia in 1967. The guided tour lasts about 90 minutes.

On weekends, head to Chatuchak Market - 15,000 stalls spread across 35 acres, 200,000 visitors daily. It's the world's largest weekend market. Take the BTS to Mo Chit or the MRT to Chatuchak Park. Arrive before 10 AM: after noon, heat and crowds make navigation difficult. Browse through sections for textiles, ceramics, vintage goods, and plants.

In the afternoon, descend to Lumphini Park - 143 acres of greenery in the heart of the business district. This Bangkok green lung hosts a colony of roughly 400 water monitors that bask by the lake or swim calmly. These lizards, which can exceed 6 feet in length, couldn't care less about visitors. Watch them from the bridges on the park's north side.

Explore the creative district of Charoen Krung and its Talad Noi alleyways - former warehouses converted into art galleries, design cafés, and workshops. It's one of Bangkok's most photogenic neighborhoods, far from standard tourist circuits. Brick facades and street art neighbor 19th-century Chinese merchant houses.

Next, head to Wat Traimit in Chinatown. It houses the world's largest solid gold Buddha - a 10-foot statue weighing 5.5 tons of pure gold. It was discovered by accident in 1955 beneath a plaster coating during relocation. The 4th-floor museum traces the story of this discovery.

Before returning to Bangkok, detour through Maeklong Railway Market, 15 minutes from Amphawa. This market has existed since 1905 on the tracks of a still-active train line. When the siren sounds, vendors fold their awnings within seconds, pull back their stalls of vegetables, fruits, and fish - and the train passes within inches of the merchandise. The ballet resumes after it passes. Trains arrive at 8:30 AM, 11:10 AM, 2:30 PM, and 5:40 PM.

activities.text: In the evening, take the MRT to Wat Mangkon station and dive into Chinatown. From 6 PM onward, Yaowarat Road transforms into an open-air food hall. Order grilled prawns or stir-fried noodles directly from a street stall, perched on a red plastic stool. The smell of durian will guide you better than any map.

In the afternoon, board a longtail boat tour of the Thonburi klongs. In one hour, you glide past wooden stilt houses, hidden temples, and gardens spilling into the canals. This is Bangkok before the skyscrapers. Tour operators offer these circuits from Tha Chang pier.

In the evening, ascend to a Bangkok rooftop - the Silom or Sathorn districts concentrate the best venues. From 650 to 1,000 feet high, the skyline ignites and the curve of the Chao Phraya glimmers in the darkness below. Reserve ahead during high season.

In the evening, pass through Khao San Road - the legendary backpacker street, roughly a third of a mile of bars, street stalls, tattoo parlors, and fried insect vendors. This isn't authentic Thailand, but it's an experience unto itself. Sample pad thai with prawns from a street stall before joining the scene.

On weekdays when not visiting Chatuchak, explore Tha Prachan Market instead, the Buddhist amulet market along the river. Thai locals come here to purchase protective statues and talismans. Atmosphere 100% local.

Book a Thai cooking class at one of the many central workshops. In 3 to 4 hours, you prepare pad thai, tom yum soup, and green curry from scratch, after a local market visit to select ingredients. Providers offer these classes in French or English.

Treat yourself to a traditional Thai massage - 60 to 90 minutes on a floor mat, dressed in pajamas. Practitioners work energy lines with stretches and pressure. Wat Pho offers sessions performed by students from its massage school.

Return to Bangkok late morning. Use these final hours for a last stroll through an unexplored neighborhood - Sathorn for colonial architecture, Si Lom for office atmosphere, or the galleries of Soi 51 in Sukhumvit if you missed the creative district.

visits.text: Far from any coast, deep in the mountains, Bo Kluea nevertheless makes its living from salt. Since the days of the Kingdom of Nan, families have drawn brine—water with a very high salt content—from wells. Bamboo pipes carry it to vats, then it is boiled over a wood fire until white crystals form. Salt is not produced during the rainy season or Buddhist Lent, the monks’ annual retreat: visit between October and February.

activities.text: Continue about ten kilometers north of Bo Kluea to the village of Sapan and its namesake waterfall. Near the waterfall, you can stay in a hut or camp in a tent. Make this detour the evening before or early in the morning, before setting off for Nan.

places.name: Chanthaburi

visits.text: Stop in front of the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception—Thailand's largest Catholic cathedral. Its 59-meter Gothic spire rises above the Chanthaburi River. Built in the 18th century and reconstructed four times, it took its current form in 1909. The French briefly occupied Chanthaburi in the late 19th century to pressure Siam—the architecture still bears traces of this. Inside is a statue of the Virgin Mary inlaid with local gemstones.

Walk along the riverfront of the historic Chanthaboon district. This 300-year-old community blends Thai wooden houses, Chinese facades and Vietnamese influences - descendants of Catholic immigrants from Vietnam still live here. The bilingual Thai-Chinese signs hanging from awnings and old teak counters give the feeling of a neighborhood frozen in the 19th century.

If you're here on a Friday, Saturday or Sunday, don't miss gem street (Si Chan Road). Over 120 shops dealing in rubies, sapphires and semi-precious stones are concentrated along a 300-meter stretch. Chanthaburi has been the global center of the ruby and sapphire trade since the 15th century—stones today come mainly from Cambodia and Burma. Traders arrive from around the world.

activities.text: Take a trip to Namtok Phlio National Park, 14 km from town. The main waterfall tumbles into a pool where 60cm fish come to feed directly underwater. The park is crossed by a forest trail that passes the steles of several Rama kings who vacationed here.

activities.text: Take a photo of the map posted at the entrance to Chatuchak Market: without it, you can quickly get lost. More than 15,000 stalls spread across 27 sections welcome over 200,000 visitors every weekend. The clock tower, built in 1987 for King Bhumibol’s 60th birthday, serves as a meeting point. The full market opens only on Saturdays and Sundays, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Arrive at 9 a.m. via Kamphaeng Phet subway station and buy some water: the aisles get very hot.

places.name: Chiang Khan

visits.text: Wake before 6am. On Chai Khong Road, monks parade in silence at dawn for alms collection - a ritual borrowed from Lao rather than Thai tradition, a vestige of ancient ties to the Lan Xang kingdom across the river. Locals lay out baskets of sticky rice and fruit on the sidewalk before the sun touches the Mekong.

Then stroll along Chai Khong Road in the morning mist. This street of two-story wooden houses runs along the Mekong for 1 km. Each building houses a guesthouse, café or craft shop. On the river side, the Lao bank lies 300 meters away. It's one of the region's best-preserved streets of wooden buildings.

3 km east of the center, Kaeng Khut Khu rapids form a succession of rocks and swift currents on the Mekong. A walkway runs along the shore. In the dry season, rocks emerge and form islands. Boats offer 30–60-minute trips to see the rapids from the water.

activities.text: In the evening, Chai Khong Road becomes a walking street from 5 p.m. The stalls offer local specialties: kai yang Chiang Khan (chicken marinated with mountain herbs from Loei and grilled over charcoal), khanom jeen (fermented rice vermicelli with curry), and sweets made with sesame and coconut. The crowd is almost exclusively Thai.

As an option, go up to Chiang Khan Skywalk, a horseshoe-shaped glass walkway built in 2020, 80 meters above the confluence of the Mekong and the Hueang River. Allow for a round trip during the day from Chiang Khan. Preferably visit early in the morning for the banks of mist over the Laotian mountains.

places.name: Chiang Mai

visits.text: Begin with Wat Chedi Luang in the old city center. Construction started in 1391 to house the ashes of King Saen Muang Ma's father and was completed in 1475 at a height of 82 m—the tallest building in the Lanna kingdom. In 1545, an earthquake destroyed the top 30 meters. The truncated structure has stood ever since. In the eastern niche, a replica of the Emerald Buddha recalls that the original spent a century here before being transferred to Bangkok. Four staircases guarded by nagas—mythical serpents—frame the four sides. Allow 45 minutes to 1 hour.

Ten minutes' walk west, Wat Phra Singh is Chiang Mai's most revered temple. Founded in 1345 by King Phayu, it houses the Phra Buddha Sihing statue - its origin remains a mystery, with some chronicles tracing it from Sri Lanka via India and Ayutthaya. Enter the Viharn Lai Kham: 19th-century murals depict daily life under the Lanna kingdom. Each April during Songkran, the statue parades through Chiang Mai's streets in procession.

Leave early for Doi Suthep—15 km from the city at an altitude of 1,073 m. The legend of its founding in 1383: a white elephant carrying a Buddha relic climbed the mountain, trumpeted three times and collapsed. The king saw this as a sign and had the temple built. Climb the 309 steps flanked by nagas or take the funicular. At the top, the 24 m golden chedi gleams in the morning sun. The view over Chiang Mai from the terrace covers the entire plain. Arrive before 9 AM to avoid groups.

activities.text: On Saturday evening, the Walking Street on Wualai Road comes to life from 5 PM. Local artisans sell repoussé silver, Bo Sang umbrellas and hill-tribe textiles—it is more local and less touristy than the standard night market. Food stalls offer khao soi (egg-noodle curry, a northern specialty) and grilled Chiang Mai sausages. Allow at least 2 hours.

For those wanting to dive deeper into local cuisine, cooking classes are offered in the old city: a morning market visit to choose ingredients, then 3–4 hours in the kitchen. Khao soi, green curry and tom kha are the classics on the menu. Book the day before.

In the afternoon, let yourself drift toward Nimman Road, Chiang Mai's neighborhood of cafés and designers. Shophouses house local designer boutiques, galleries, coworking spaces and specialty coffee shops—coffee from the northern mountains is a source of regional pride. One Nimman, the complex on the corner, brings together craft shops, restaurants and smoothie bars. It's also a good place to find hill-tribe textiles, celadon pottery and bamboo baskets.

places.name: Chiang Rai

visits.text: 13 km south of Chiang Rai, Wat Rong Khun—the White Temple—is entirely covered in white plaster inlaid with thousands of mirror fragments. Approach via the Sukavadee Bridge: on each side, hands reaching skyward emerge from the ground, symbols of souls who haven't reached nirvana. Artist Chalermchai Kositpipat funded and built it himself, with work begun in the late 1990s and still ongoing. Inside, the frescoes blend Buddhist scenes with pop culture characters—Batman, Neo from The Matrix. Photos are forbidden in the main building.

The Baan Dam Museum, 10 km north of the city center, is the exact opposite of the White Temple. Forty dark wooden buildings arranged in a garden—the work of national artist Thawan Duchanee. He used animal skins, skulls, buffalo horns. The ensemble explores themes of death and the cycle of life in Buddhist philosophy.

End the day at Wat Rong Suea Ten, the Blue Temple, 6 km north of the center. The main hall is entirely painted in a shade between sapphire and cerulean, with a large white seated Buddha at the back. The name means “temple of the dancing tiger”—tigers allegedly once leapt through the abandoned ruins.

Head down to the confluence of the Mekong and Ruak rivers at Sop Ruak. This is where the Thai, Burmese and Lao borders meet—the historic Golden Triangle. Thailand eradicated poppy cultivation on its territory as early as the 1970s and 1980s through royal crop substitution programs. Across the border in Myanmar, production continued well beyond that period. A golden Buddha statue stands on a boat-shaped platform moored beside the Mekong. From the bank, look towards Laos on the right and Burma on the left. Allow for a day trip from Chiang Rai.

About 2 km north of Sop Ruak, the Hall of Opium traces the history of the drug in the region, from its medical uses in the nineteenth century to its eradication. The museum is one of the country's most modern - allow two hours. It is closed on Mondays. From Chiang Rai, allow approximately 80 km and 1 hour 30 minutes by road to reach it.

Back in Chiang Rai, push through the door of Wat Phra Kaew—this is where the Emerald Buddha was discovered in 1434 inside a stucco-covered chedi. Lightning had split the stucco, revealing the green jade. The statue then departed for Lampang, Chiang Mai, and finally Bangkok. A replica remains here.

activities.text: In the evening, wander through Chiang Rai's Night Bazaar, south of the city center. Karen tribe stalls, Hmong embroidery, mountain coffee. Order naem ngiao—the spicy pork and tomato soup, a northern specialty often missing from Chiang Mai menus.
Take a short long-tail boat trip on the Mekong from Sop Ruak—you follow the Burmese bank and approach the Lao island of Don Sao. Allow for a day trip from Chiang Rai.

visits.text: The best time to visit Wat Sirindhorn Wararam Phu Prao, near Chong Mek, is after dark. A large Tree of Life is painted with phosphorescent pigment on the back wall of the ordination hall. This pigment absorbs daylight, then releases it in the dark, without any lamps. The design begins to glow around 7:30 PM. Arrive an hour before sunset to see the temple in daylight, then wait. The temple closes around 8 PM, and admission is free: bring a flashlight for the way back.

visits.text: Head down to Hat Thung Wua Laen, the best beach on the Chumphon coast; allow for a round trip by road from Chumphon. This 2.7-kilometer ribbon of white sand runs alongside a quiet road lined with bungalows and small restaurants. Its name means 'beach of the running bison' - a relic of the days when herds grazed here. On weekdays, you will have it almost to yourself.

Climb up to Khao Matsee Viewpoint late in the day. The overlook commands views of the coastline and the national park's offshore islands. A café with a terrace awaits you at the summit—the perfect spot to watch the sun sink over the Gulf of Thailand.

activities.text: Drive from Hua Hin or Bangkok to Chumphon (3.5 hours from Hua Hin, around 500 km from Bangkok). Chumphon is also a stop on the Bangkok–Surat Thani overnight train — arrival possible in the early morning.

In the evening, explore Chumphon's night market, set up in the town center. The stalls selling tropical fruit from local orchards are particularly well stocked—mangosteens, durians and rambutans depending on the season.

places.name: Doi Inthanon

visits.text: First stop climbing toward the summit: Wachirathan Waterfall, whose name means “diamond stream.” Water plunges 70 meters down a granite escarpment. In good weather, a permanent rainbow forms at the base. This is the most powerful waterfall in the park.

At 2,560 meters altitude, the twin pagodas dominate the surrounding valleys. The first, Naphamethinidon, was erected in 1987 for King Bhumibol's 60th birthday. The second, Naphaphonphumisiri, in 1992 for Queen Sirikit's 60th birthday. Their flowered gardens change color with the seasons—Siamese cherry blossoms from late January to early February.

Continue to Thailand's highest point: 2,565 meters. In January, it averages 6°C here. The Ang Ka trail takes you along a 360-meter boardwalk above a marsh of moss and orchids. This is one of the few places in Thailand where you can spot Himalayan bird species.

activities.text: If you're here between November and March, take the Kew Mae Pan trail—a 3 km loop through conifer forest and highland savanna, with views across the Burmese ridges. Bring a jacket: temperatures can drop to 5°C in the morning.

visits.text: The Nan and Pua rivers rise in Doi Phu Kha National Park, which has protected around 1,700 km² since 1999. The park takes its name from Doi Phu Kha, a 1,980 m peak. On the road from Pua to Bo Kluea, about 5 km from the park headquarters, a viewpoint overlooks the ridges. Admission: 200 baht per foreign adult.

activities.text: Clusters of pink flowers identify the chomphu phu kha, a rare tree that grows nowhere else in Thailand outside this park. It blooms from January to early March, especially in February. The nature trail named after it forms a 2 km loop that takes about 1 hour 30 minutes to walk. The longer 4 km loop takes 3 hours.

visits.text: A Western lady in a Victorian dress wearing a Thai crown: that is how Chakri Maha Prasat, the Grand Palace’s main throne hall, is sometimes described. The lower part of the building is European, while its roofs are Thai. The palace has been the official residence of the kings since 1782, but the current king lives in another palace, Dusit Palace. Arrive when it opens at 8:30 AM. If a stranger tells you the palace is closed today, it is a well-known scam: he wants to take you elsewhere in a tuk-tuk. Do not follow him.

Twelve giants standing about 5 m tall, the yaksha (guardian demons from Indian mythology), watch over the gates of Wat Phra Kaew, the Grand Palace’s royal chapel. Inside, the Emerald Buddha measures only about 66 cm. It is carved not from emerald but from a green stone often described as jade. Three times a year, during a royal ceremony, its gold attire is changed to mark the new season. The 500-baht ticket covers the palace and the chapel. Tank tops, shorts, and tight or ripped pants are not allowed: visitors wearing them are denied entry.

visits.text: Head to Mrigadayavan Palace, 7.5 miles north of Hua Hin. Built in 1924 by Italian architect Ercole Manfreddy for King Rama VI, this summer palace is entirely golden teak on stilts, connected by 3,280 feet of aerial walkways. Eighteen pavilions face the sea - the sea breeze circulates beneath the wooden floors. Walk barefoot on the walkways and gaze at the Gulf of Thailand horizon.

Late afternoon, climb Khao Takiab hill south of the beach. A large golden Buddha faces the sea from the summit. Macaques occupy the stairways - stay alert with your belongings. The view over Hua Hin bay and the long sand strip is one of the coast's finest.

activities.text: In the evening, descend to Hua Hin Night Market, intersection of Dechanuchit and Phetkasem Road. After 6:30 PM, seafood stalls invade the street - giant prawns, lobsters, whole fish on charcoal. Grill smoke, mango stall colors, vendors calling out - it's the bustle of popular Thailand, Gulf coast version.

visits.text: A museum of traditional Thai houses, created by an American: this is the Jim Thompson House. After settling in Bangkok, Thompson founded a silk company there in 1948. In 1958, he had six 19th-century wooden houses, mostly from Ayutthaya, reassembled here. The largest, a weaver’s house, came from Bangkrua, across the canal, where his weavers worked. Thompson disappeared in Malaysia in 1967. Visits are by guided tour, lasting about 30 minutes and also available in French: admission is 250 baht, with opening hours from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Remove your shoes at each threshold.

places.name: Kanchanaburi

visits.text: Walk across the Bridge on the River Kwai. This steel bridge built in 1943 by the Japanese army forms part of the infamous Death Railway - 258 miles from Thailand into Burma, constructed in 17 months at the cost of 100,000 deaths including 15,000 Allied prisoners. The angular central spans were rebuilt after Allied bombing in 1945. A passenger train still crosses it twice daily at walking speed.

Head to the JEATH War Museum, south of the town centre, on the riverbank. JEATH is the acronym for Japan, England, Australia, Thailand, Holland - the nationalities involved in building the railway. This small museum, founded in 1977 by a Thai monk, displays artefacts, prisoners' tools, period photographs and reconstructions of bamboo barracks. Its raw presentation makes the suffering more tangible than any large modern museum.

Walk to Kanchanaburi War Cemetery (Don Rak). Beneath flowering frangipani trees, 6,982 perfectly aligned headstones mark the graves of Allied prisoners who died on the construction site. The inscriptions - ages, regiments, words from their families - put a human face on the numbers.

Take the bus from Kanchanaburi terminal to reach Erawan National Park (90-minute drive). This 212-square-mile park takes its name from the mythological three-headed elephant of Hindu cosmology. Its waterfall unfolds in 7 successive tiers. At tier 2, the turquoise basin is deep and swimmable - small fish will nibble your dead skin, a completely free fish spa. From tier 4 onward, passages steepen. Tier 7 is the reward: a taller cascade in a setting enclosed by limestone cliffs.

Take the train from Kanchanaburi (departure around 6 AM, 100 baht for foreigners). After the bridge over the River Kwai, the line enters the forest and hugs limestone cliffs. Get off at Tham Krasae stop. The 1,475-foot wooden viaduct clings to the cliff face above the Khwae Noi River - you can walk across it. A cave temple nearby sheltered sick prisoners of war.

From Nam Tok, take a songthaew to Hellfire Pass Memorial Museum (50 miles northwest of Kanchanaburi). This site managed by the Australian government traces the construction of the railway's deadliest section - a 246-foot cutting through solid rock, hand-carved. At night, by torchlight, prisoners became shadows in the flames - hence the name 'Hellfire Pass'. The museum is free, understated, and gripping.

activities.text: Late afternoon, walk or cycle along the Kwai River. The town is pleasant in the evening - waterfront terraces on stilts, fresh fish restaurants, quiet bars. Tour operators offer longtail boat rides on the river, between karsts and forests.

Swim in the emerald pools at tiers 2 and 3. Arrive early (opens at 8 AM) to avoid weekend crowds. After tier 2, food and drinks are prohibited - eat before ascending. Bring a life jacket (rental on-site) if entering deep pools.
Walk the Hellfire Pass trail - nearly a mile through the rock cutting. You touch the tool marks still visible on the walls. The place is silent. Panels recount survivors' testimonies. Take your time.

places.name: Khao Lak

visits.text: Visit the tsunami memorial on Highway 4, north of Khao Lak. A police boat — number 813 — rests there, carried 2 km inland by the wave of December 26, 2004. This boat belonged to the Royal Thai Navy and was at sea that morning. Khao Lak recorded the highest run-up wave ever measured in Thailand that day.

Walk along Nang Thong Beach and Bang Niang Beach, Khao Lak's two main beaches. A post-tsunami regulation bans high-rise construction along the shoreline — result: no towers, no concrete dominating the sea, just discreet resorts in the trees. Khao Lak Beach stretches 16 km in total.

activities.text: Drive Khao Sok to Khao Lak (around 1.5 hours). Khao Lak is the departure point for excursions to the Similan Islands, accessible only from October to May from Thap Lamu pier. Off-season, inquire about snorkeling trips around the coastal islands.

If you are here between November and April, book a snorkeling trip to the Similan Islands from Thap Lamu Pier (60 km offshore). The Similans are among Asia's ten best diving sites - multicolored corals, manta rays and whitetip sharks. The park closes from mid-May to mid-October.

places.name: Khao Sok

visits.text: Check into a bungalow beside the Sok River, at the entrance to the national park. The forest surrounding you is estimated to be over 160 million years old—older and richer in biodiversity than the Amazon. As you make your way down to your lodging, listen: male gibbons give their territorial calls from dawn.

Set off hiking the park trails late in the afternoon, when light filters through the canopy. The park is home to wild elephants, Malayan sun bears, tapirs, and clouded leopards. Between January and March, the rafflesia can bloom here — its flower reaches up to 80 cm in diameter, one of the largest in the world.

Board a longtail boat on Cheow Lan Lake at Ratchaprapha Pier, approximately 65 km from Khao Sok village, a 1-hour drive. The lake, created by the dam of the same name in 1986, covers 165 km² in the heart of the forest. The limestone karsts - some reaching 960 meters - plunge straight into the emerald water. First stop: Khao Sam Kloe, a trio of limestone towers rising from the water, which Thai people nickname 'the Guilin of Cheow Lan'.
Explore Phra Kay Petch Cave, 100 meters long, which opens onto the Klong Ka tributary. Inside, colored stalactites and stalagmites descend into the darkness. Thousands of bats roost on the ceiling.

activities.text: Drive from Ranong to Khao Sok (around 3 hours) via Highway 4 then Route 401. Along the way, you'll pass through rubber and oil palm plantations that blanket the southern hills. Arrive in the afternoon to enjoy the forest light.
Night safari on the park trails with a local guide. The forest reveals itself most at night: slow lorises, palm civets, frogs of improbable size. Bring a headlamp and closed-toe shoes.

Full-day longtail excursion on Cheow Lan Lake from Ratchaprapha Pier, approximately 65 km from Khao Sok village, a 1-hour drive. Book the day before through your accommodation. Leave early - morning mist wraps around the karsts and the light is perfect before 9 a.m.

Kayak from the floating bungalows: paddle among the limestone islets in absolute calm. Most accommodations on the water provide kayaks to their guests. Early in the morning, watch for monkeys in the treetops along the shores.

places.name: Khao Yai

visits.text: Pass through the gate of Khao Yai National Park—2,168 km² of tropical forest, UNESCO-listed in 2005, Thailand's first national park, established in 1962. Start at the visitor center to pick up a trail map and choose your guide. Seven official trails wind through the park; most require a guide.

Make your way down alongside the 150-meter Haew Narok waterfall, the park's highest, which plunges in three tiers through the jungle. The path from the parking area runs 600 meters. On the surrounding cliffs, red orchids (Renanthera) give the falls their name—“Haew Narok” means “ravine of hell”. Wild elephants frequent the area—stay on the trail.

At dusk, head to Nong Phak Chi grassland. This is where great hornbills emerge from the trees to feed. Khao Yai shelters four hornbill species and one of the region's largest populations of white-handed gibbons. Settle in and wait - sambar deer and pig-tailed macaques often appear before dark.

Head down to Haew Suwat waterfall, a 20-meter drop into a sandstone pool encircled by jungle. This is where Leonardo DiCaprio and his companions jumped in the film "The Beach" (2000). The scene of the leap into the lagoon was actually filmed at Koh Phi Phi - but the waterfall itself is real. Take the short trail (100 meters from the road) and descend the steps to water level.

Continue on foot to Pha Kluai Mai Waterfall. Less conspicuous and much less visited, it borders the campsite of the same name. A rope bridge crosses the Lam Ta Khong River. The atmosphere is peaceful, especially on weekdays.

activities.text: Take a guided hike along one of the marked forest trails (allow 3 to 5 hours depending on the route). Guides available through operators in Pak Chong know how to read elephant tracks and locate gibbons by their calls.
An optional evening activity: a guided night safari in a 4x4. With a spotlight and patience, you can spot civets, hares, barking deer and sometimes a sun bear in the vegetation.

In the afternoon, leave the park to explore the vineyards that have developed in the hills around Pak Chong since the 1990s. PB Valley Khao Yai Winery and GranMonte are the two best-known wineries. The climatic conditions at altitude (600–800 m) allow varieties like Shiraz and Chenin Blanc to be grown in a tropical climate—a rare viticultural curiosity in Asia.

Wake up early (6 a.m.) and head to Lam Ta Khong Campsite in Khao Yai National Park. Its meadow borders the river: watch deer in the open areas and birds along the banks, keeping your distance from the animals. Follow the paths through the campsite for a morning walk.

places.name: Khlong Bang Luang

visits.text: The Artist’s House (Baan Silapin) is an L-shaped wooden house on the banks of Khlong Bang Luang. This canal is also known as Khlong Bangkok Yai. The name Bang Luang recalls the nobles who settled along its banks in the 18th century, under King Taksin. Upstairs is a gallery, while the ground floor has souvenirs and craft workshops. Admission is free, from 10 AM to 6 PM: ask your boat operator to stop for half an hour.

activities.text: If you want to see Bangkok from its canals, hire a long-tail boat, a narrow motorboat, at Tha Chang Pier near the Grand Palace. It takes you into the khlongs of Thonburi, the canals on the west bank. Khlong Bangkok Yai was once the riverbed. In the 16th century, a king of the Kingdom of Ayutthaya had a shortcut dug to bypass this long bend, and the Chao Phraya took this new route. Expect to pay 2,000 to 2,800 baht per boat for two hours, and agree on the route and price before boarding.

places.name: Khon Kaen

visits.text: Visit Khon Kaen National Museum, one of Isan's richest museums. It presents finds from regional excavations: Bronze Age pottery, iron tools and copper jewelry from sites near Ban Chiang and in the surrounding area. The archaeological context of the Khorat Plateau is well explained here.

Climb the nine stories of Wat Phra That Kaen Nakhon on the shores of Bueng Kaen Nakhon Lake. Each level of the chedi is decorated with carved panels illustrating episodes from the Buddha's life. The view from the top takes in the lake, parks and the entire city.

activities.text: In the evening, head to Ton Tann night market, the largest in Khon Kaen. Try larb moo - minced pork mixed with fresh mint, lime juice and roasted ground rice, served at room temperature. It's the emblematic dish of northeastern Thailand, spicy and bright, worlds away from central Thai cuisine.
Cycle or walk around Bueng Kaen Nakhon Lake. The route runs about 4 km and passes public gardens, temples and waterfront cafés. It's where locals stroll in late afternoon.

visits.text: Khong Chiam residents have a saying for the meeting of the Mekong and the Mun River: “Khong si poon, Mun si khram”—the Mekong is chalky red, the Mun indigo blue. During the rainy season, the Mekong carries large amounts of silt and turns reddish brown. The Mun, held back a little downstream by the Pak Mun Dam, remains clearer, with a blue-green hue. A distinct line then separates the two waters. During the dry season, it is less noticeable. The best viewpoint is the riverbank at Wat Khong Chiam in the late morning.

Rows of seated Buddhas, a reclining Buddha, and a view down over Laos: Wat Tham Khuha Sawan occupies a cliff at a bend in Route 2222, just before Khong Chiam. In this cave temple, the remains of the monk Luang Pu Kam Khaning Chula Mani, a meditation master, rest in a glass coffin. A giant gong greets visitors at the entrance. The site is always open and admission is free, but wear clothing that provides adequate coverage.

In September and October, a waterfall cascades down the cliff just above Wat Tham Hew Sin Chai, a temple built beneath a rocky overhang near Khong Chiam. In April, it is too dry to see the waterfall. During the dry season, come instead for the temple sheltered beneath the rock. The site is open from 8:30 AM to 6 PM, and admission is free.

activities.text: You can reach the confluence by long-tail boat from the riverbank in Khong Chiam. A few boat operators offer the trip, with prices arranged on-site. During the dry season, low water reveals small wooded islands near the confluence. The boat also takes you right up to the line between the two colors. Agree on the price and duration before boarding.

places.name: Ko Pha Ngan

visits.text: Thirty-minute ferry from Samui. Arrival at Thong Sala, Koh Pha Ngan's main port. Rent a scooter at the pier - it's the only practical way to explore the island. Roads are decent on the west coast, more adventurous on the east and north.

Start with Phaeng Noi waterfall, in the island's center, in Than Sadet National Park. A 500-meter trail leads to a waterfall surrounded by dense jungle. Continuing 30 minutes upward, a viewpoint offers views over the entire west coast and distant islands. Entry 100 baht.

Leave early for Bottle Beach (Haad Khuat), on the north coast. Two options: a 2.5 km jungle trail from Chaloklum (1h30, steep) or a taxi-boat from Chaloklum (10 min, 100 baht). The beach is a white sand crescent framed by boulders and coconut palms - no road, no cars, just a few wooden bungalows. It's the image you have in mind when you think “Thai beach”.

Late afternoon, ride to Mae Haad Beach on the northwest coast. At low tide, a sandbar connects Koh Pha Ngan to the small island of Koh Ma. Cross on foot - ankle-deep water - to the island. Decent snorkeling around rocks on the north side. Check tide times before going.

Ride toward the east coast to Than Sadet National Park. The eponymous waterfall flows over granite rocks carved by several Rama kings - Rama V came to bathe here in the late 19th century. Descending the rocks to natural pools takes 20 minutes. Continue to Haad Sadet Beach, a wild beach with two bars and deep water for swimming.

Push on to Thong Nai Pan, the northeast's double bay. Two crescent beaches separated by a rocky headland - Thong Nai Pan Noi (the small one) is quieter, Thong Nai Pan Yai (the big one) has more restaurants. Access via a winding road from the island's center makes it less crowded than the west coast.

Head down to Haad Rin, at the southern tip of the island. This peninsula has two beaches: Haad Rin Nok (on the east side, the Full Moon Party beach) and Rin Nai (on the west side, for sunsets). Outside party periods, Haad Rin Nok is a lovely fine-sand beach with clear water.
Stop at the Kuan Yin Chinese temple. A large statue of Guanyin looks out to sea from a dragon-adorned terrace. The temple is more recent but photogenic - and almost always empty.

activities.text: Settle into Srithanu on the west coast, the island's yoga and wellness quarter. Relaxed vibe, vegetarian cafés, beachfront yoga studios. It's not for everyone, but it's Koh Pha Ngan's alternative face, far from Haad Rin's parties.

Lunch at the fishing village of Chaloklum, at the back of the north bay. Restaurants serve the morning's catch - grilled sea bass, prawns sautéed with basil, tom yum soup. Chaloklum has remained a real fishing port, with colorful boats at anchor and nets drying on the pier.

Take a taxi-boat from Haad Rin to Haad Yuan, the hidden beach on the southeast coast. No road: you arrive by boat or via a 2h trek through jungle. A few wooden bungalows, a bar perched on rocks (Eden Bar), and turquoise water. On Saturday nights, Eden Bar hosts a party that runs until Sunday morning - electronic music vibe in the middle of nature.

In the evening, dine at Thong Sala's Phantip Night Market. It's the island's real local market - pad thai, chicken skewers, sticky mango rice, fresh fruit juices. Thais eat there between 6 pm and 9 pm. Less photogenic than Fisherman's Village, but more authentic.

places.name: Ko Samui

visits.text: Cross the causeway that connects Koh Samui to the islet of Koh Faan. At the end stands the Big Buddha - 12 meters tall, golden, seated in the Mara posture - staring back at you since 1972. It's often the first thing you spot when landing in Samui. Climb the bell-lined staircase. At the top, views sweep across the entire Bang Rak bay and planes taking off 3 km away.

Two kilometers from Big Buddha, push on to Wat Plai Laem. This modern temple built on an artificial lake blends Chinese and Thai styles. The 18-armed white statue of Guanyin reflects in the water. Catfish in the lake fight over pellets visitors toss them. It's more kitsch than solemn - and that's precisely its charm.

Board at 7:30 am from Nathon pier for Ang Thong Marine Park - 42 limestone islands set on an emerald-green sea, 30 km northwest of Samui. The boat docks at Wua Talap, the main island. Climb the 500 steps up to the viewpoint: below, the archipelago spreads like a scale model - jungle-covered islets, turquoise lagoons, deserted white beaches.

Take the boat to Mae Koh island. A 400-meter trail climbs through jungle to the Thale Nai - the Emerald Lake. This inland saltwater lagoon, ringed by limestone cliffs, shifts color with the light. In the morning, it's deep green. It's the most famous image of Ang Thong, and it doesn't disappoint.

Stop by Wat Khunaram in the central hills. Monk Luong Pordaeng died in 1973 in meditation position. His mummified body is displayed in a glass case - seated, sunglasses on, barely altered after 50 years. For Thai Buddhists, it's a sign of extreme virtue. The place is understated and peaceful.

Continue to Na Muang 1 waterfall, accessible in 5 minutes' walk from the parking lot. Water drops 18 meters into a natural pool of purple granite - the color gives the waterfall its name (na muang = purple water). Swimming possible during rainy season when the flow is strong.

If you have a 4x4 or powerful scooter, climb to the Secret Buddha Garden, at 500 meters altitude in the jungle. This sculpture garden was created in 1976 by a farmer, Nim Thongsuk, who spent 20 years erecting Buddha and goddess statues among the trees. The road up is steep, muddy after rain, and not for scooter beginners.

Give yourself a morning at Chaweng, Samui's main beach - 5 km of white sand, shallow water, coconut palms. It's the island's busiest and makes no apologies: parasols, fruit vendors, music. Swim early morning when the beach is still calm.

In the afternoon, ride to Nathon, the small administrative capital on the west coast. No tourism here - just shopping streets, a fish market, Chinese shophouses and the main ferry port. Order an iced coffee in one of the old waterfront cafés.

activities.text: Late afternoon, head down to Bophut's Fisherman's Village. This converted fishing quarter lines wooden Chinese shophouses along a calm beach. On Friday nights, the Walking Street comes alive: stalls of grilled fish, smoothies, artisan jewelry. It's the island's most pleasant market - more intimate than Chaweng, without the blasting music.

Kayak between Ang Thong's islets. Paddle into sea caves accessible at low tide and along cliffs where sea eagles nest. Most excursions include kayaking, snorkeling and lunch on Wua Talap beach. Return around 5 pm.

End the day at Lamai Beach, Samui's second beach. Calmer and longer than Chaweng, it stretches 4 km. At the south end, the rocks Hin Ta and Hin Yai (grandfather and grandmother) have very explicit anatomical shapes - Thais love posing there for photos. Dinner with your feet in the sand at one of the beach restaurants.

Sunset at Lipa Noi, the west coast beach. It faces due west, toward the mainland hills. The water is so shallow you walk 100 meters into the sea and still have water at knee level. The late-day colors - orange, pink, purple - are among Samui's finest.

places.name: Ko Tao

visits.text: Ferry from Koh Pha Ngan (1h30). Arrival at Mae Haad port. Settle into Sairee Beach, the main beach - 1.7 km of sand on the west coast. Dive schools line the beach. Koh Tao is the world's most popular place to get your PADI Open Water - prices are among the planet's lowest and conditions ideal for beginners.

Take a longtail from Mae Haad to Koh Nang Yuan, 1 km northwest. Three islets connected by two white sandbars in a Y shape. Climb the steps to the viewpoint: the plunging view over the three sand strips and turquoise water is one of the most famous images of the Gulf of Thailand. Decent snorkeling on the west side. Paid entry, no plastic allowed on the island.

Dive day. Koh Tao has 26 dive sites around the island. For beginners, Japanese Gardens offers coral gardens at 5-12 meters depth with clownfish, angelfish and stingrays. Twins, two twin pinnacles covered in corals, is perfect for a first dive. Dive schools pick up divers directly from Sairee beach.

In the afternoon, head down to Shark Bay (Thian Og Bay) south of the island. The name comes from blacktip reef sharks patrolling the shallow waters - harmless, between 1 and 2 meters long. You see them from the beach, often late in the day. Easy snorkeling from shore.

A second day underwater - the advanced sites. Sail Rock, halfway between Koh Tao and Koh Pha Ngan, is regarded as the Gulf of Thailand's best dive site. A granite pinnacle breaks the surface, with a vertical chimney divers swim through at 18 meters. Schools of barracuda, giant groupers and, in season (March-May and September-October), whale sharks. The trip takes a full day - breakfast and lunch included.

Explore the east coast by scooter. First stop: Tanote Bay, a bay wedged between granite boulders with a natural diving rock. Water is crystal clear and reefs start 2 meters from shore. Continue to Ao Leuk, a calmer bay with a gentle slope of sand and corals - perfect for a final snorkeling session.

activities.text: Late afternoon, climb to John Suwan Viewpoint at the island's southern tip. The trail starts from Chalok Baan Kao beach and climbs 20 minutes through rocks. At the top, views embrace the entire Chalok bay and Shark Bay below. It's Koh Tao's best sunset spot.

If you prefer snorkeling to scuba diving, rent a mask and fins at Sairee and reach Mango Bay and Hin Wong Bay by boat, or take the paths across the island on foot. The reefs are close to shore and visibility is often excellent. Hin Wong has large underwater rocks covered in colorful coral.

An alternative if Sail Rock is too far away or conditions are poor: Chumphon Pinnacle, 12 km to the northwest. Granite pinnacles between 12 and 35 meters deep, covered with anemones. You may encounter a whale shark there near Koh Tao. Southwest Pinnacle, 13 km to the southwest, has walls of soft coral and schools of barracuda.

Last sunset on Sairee Beach. Beach bars roll out their cushions on the sand and musicians settle in. It's the end-of-trip vibe - feet in the sand, cold beer, the sun dropping into the Gulf. For the return journey, ferries to Chumphon (mainland, 2h) or back via Koh Pha Ngan and Samui.

places.name: Koh Chang

visits.text: Take the ferry from Laem Ngop pier (45-minute crossing). On Koh Chang, start with Bang Bao village at the southern tip - a fishing village built entirely on stilts over the bay. Wooden houses are connected by walkways. Restaurants and dive operators have set up shop, but the village's original character remains intact.
Head back up toward the west coast to Lonely Beach. A kilometer of sand between jungle-covered hills. The road runs above it - you need to walk down. Accommodation here is simple and inexpensive.

Make your way to Klong Plu waterfall in the national forest, accessible from Klong Prao beach. A well-defined 600-meter trail leads to a 30-meter waterfall plunging into a swimming hole carved in sandstone. Fish swim about in the clear waters. Arrive before 9 a.m. to avoid organized groups.

Take a day trip to Koh Wai—45 minutes by boat from Bang Bao. This small 3 km² island has no roads or electricity from the grid. The coral is in good condition, especially on the northeast side. You can snorkel directly from the sand without needing another boat.

An alternative: Koh Mak, a 16 km² island. Quiet, sparsely populated and without jet skis - agencies on Koh Chang organize day trips combining beach time, snorkeling and a visit to the small fishing village.

Enjoy the morning on the island before catching the ferry. Koh Chang is also worth exploring by bicycle on the east coast, much calmer than the touristy west: deserted beaches, a few fishing villages, and direct views of Koh Mak and Koh Kood islands on the horizon.

activities.text: From Bang Bao, take a boat tour around the south of the island. Pier operators offer excursions to the islets of Koh Rang and Koh Kluay, with snorkeling on reefs that are still relatively undisturbed. Visibility can reach 15 to 20 meters in the dry season.

If you stay on Koh Chang: rent a kayak in Salak Phet Bay on the east side of the island. This enclosed bay is bordered by mangroves 10 to 15 meters high. You paddle between aerial roots, spotting fiddler crabs and gray herons. Operators also offer guided sunset outings.
Take the ferry back to Laem Ngop mid-morning, then drive to Bangkok (about 5 hours) or take a flight from Trat airport, 40 km from Laem Ngop. You'll arrive in Bangkok in the evening.

places.name: Koh Lanta

visits.text: Arrive at Koh Lanta by ferry from Krabi. Get settled, then head down to Lanta Old Town, on the island's east coast. Its century-old teak houses stand on stilts in what was once a Chinese trading post on the maritime route between Phuket, Penang, and Singapore. The inhabitants: Thai Chinese, Thai Muslims, and Chao Lay (sea nomads). Have lunch at one of the wooden restaurants whose tables overlook the sea.

Head down to the southern tip of the island to enter Mu Ko Lanta National Park. Short hike to the lighthouse—it stands at the end of a headland plunging into the Andaman Sea. Around you, dense jungle and reefs visible through the transparent water.

Take a longtail to Koh Rok, 47 km south of Koh Lanta. This pair of uninhabited islands in the Mu Ko Lanta marine park is one of the region's finest snorkeling spots: 20–25 meters of underwater visibility, corals in excellent condition, sea turtles regularly sighted.

activities.text: Ferry Krabi to Koh Lanta from Ao Nang or Krabi Town pier. The crossing takes around 2 hours depending on the boat type. Upon arrival, rent a scooter in Saladan — it's the best way to explore the island at your own pace.
Sunset from Kantiang Bay, on the island's south. This long, lightly frequented bay offers Koh Lanta's most peaceful panorama — a few terraced resorts and a nearly deserted beach in low season.
Snorkeling around Koh Rok: gear up on the boat and explore the reefs in open water. Operators based on Koh Lanta organize small-group trips—departure at 8:30 a.m., return around 4 p.m.
In the evening, return to Long Beach or Klong Dao Beach for sunset. Koh Lanta faces due west — sunsets over the Andaman Sea are among the most beautiful on the Thai coast.

places.name: Koh Lipe

visits.text: Disembark at Pattaya Beach from the speedboat arriving from Pak Bara. Koh Lipe is Thailand's southernmost island—30 km from Langkawi, Malaysia. It measures barely 4 km² and can be explored entirely on foot. Walk along Walking Street, the pedestrian thoroughfare linking Pattaya Beach to Sunrise Beach in 15 minutes: swimsuit shops, beachfront restaurants, fruit vendors, masseurs. Laid-back vibe, no cars.

Settle in on Sunrise Beach (Hat Chao Ley) in the late afternoon. It's the island regulars' favorite beach—finer sand, calmer water, views of the small islets of Koh Kra and Koh Usen. Opposite, the large island of Koh Adang bounds the horizon to the north.

Take the boat taxi from Sunrise Beach to Koh Adang (10 minutes). The island is jungle-covered and nearly deserted. Three viewpoints lie along the trail as you climb: the first is reached in 15 minutes, the last—Chado Hill—in 45 to 60 minutes. From the summit, Koh Lipe appears in its entirety, ringed by turquoise reefs. It's the journey's final panorama.
Last swim at Sunset Beach, a 15-minute walk west of Walking Street. The beach faces the Malaysian horizon. A few rocks on the south side harbor corals accessible by swimming at high tide.

activities.text: Speedboat from Pak Bara Pier to Koh Lipe (1 hour 30 minutes). Pak Bara Pier is approximately 102 km from Trang, a 1-hour-40-minute drive. Arrive at the pier early in the morning - boats generally leave between 9 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. A ferry also runs directly from Koh Lipe to Langkawi (Malaysia).

Snorkeling from Sunrise Beach: two islets (Koh Kra and Koh Usen) are reachable by kayak in 20 minutes. Corals, clownfish, and giant clams just a few meters below the surface. Rent a mask and fins directly on the beach.

Kayak around the small islets off Sunrise Beach: Koh Kra and Koh Usen. Allow 3 hours to complete the full circuit. The water is so clear that you paddle above the corals without having to dive. Rental operators are right on Sunrise Beach.

For the return: speedboat to Pak Bara, then travel by road to Hat Yai (domestic airport) or Trang (train station). From Koh Lipe, it's also possible to reach Langkawi in Malaysia directly by ferry to continue the journey south.

visits.text: Ferry from Krabi Town or Ao Nang to Koh Phi Phi Don (approximately 1.5 hours). Upon arrival at Tonsai Village, drop your bags and climb to the viewpoint. Expect 343 steps to the first lookout—a few dozen more to the second. At the top: the view of Phi Phi's two bays, Tonsai Bay on the left, Loh Dalum Bay on the right, and the limestone cliffs enclosing them. It's the only spot on the island where you truly grasp its geography—a 150 m strip of land between two bays. Sunrise or late afternoon for the best light.

Leave before 8 AM for the Maya Bay excursion. The beach on Phi Phi Leh was made famous by Danny Boyle's film The Beach (2000) with Leonardo DiCaprio. Closed for four years to recover from overcrowding, it reopened in 2022 with strict rules: no swimming, stays limited to 1 hour, access via a floating dock at Loh Samah Bay followed by a 10-minute walk. Cliffs enclose the white sand beach—it's dizzying. The bay closes in August and September every year. Advance booking is essential; opt for an early departure.

activities.text: Evenings on Phi Phi Don are lively, but there's more to them than partying. Tonsai Village offers restaurants on stilts, beachside cocktail bars and live music on Loh Dalum beach. Eat grilled fish by the water, drink a cocktail from a coconut shell. Things get livelier around 10 PM—it's an island of backpackers and divers, with a relaxed atmosphere.

The excursion generally includes Bamboo Island (Koh Mai Phai): a flat island, a strip of white sand and crystal-clear water perfect for swimming. And Shark Point for snorkeling—blacktip sharks are common and harmless there, swimming at depths of 2–3 m above the coral. Local operators combine Maya Bay, Bamboo Island and Shark Point in one day.

visits.text: Arrival at Krabi Airport (KBV), then transfer to Ao Nang - the ideal base, reached by taxi; also allow for a road journey from Krabi Town if you are staying there. It is the most accessible beach in the region: karst cliffs plunge straight into the turquoise water of the Andaman Sea. Longtail boats at anchor, traders by the water, coconut stalls. This is a transit day - get settled and explore the waterfront.

Board a longtail from Ao Nang (15-minute crossing) for Railay. This peninsula is cut off from the mainland by vertical limestone cliffs—accessible only by sea. West Railay on the beach side, East Railay on the mangrove side, and at the end of the path Phra Nang beach, framed by rock pillars rising from the water. Phra Nang cave houses a shrine to the fishermen's goddess—an altar laden with floral offerings and votive phalluses, a thousand-year tradition among the region's sailors. Railay's cliffs are one of Southeast Asia's most renowned climbing spots. Operators offer introductory day courses.

In the late afternoon, return to Krabi Town for Tiger Cave Temple. The main temple sits at the foot of the hill. But the summit is worth the detour: 1,237 steep steps through the jungle, watched over by macaques. At the top, a golden Buddha, a chedi and panoramic views over the Krabi plain, the limestone cliffs and the Andaman Sea in the distance. Go late in the day to avoid the heat—and allow 1.5 hours for the round trip.

activities.text: In the evening, dine on Ao Nang beach: several restaurants set their tables directly on the sand with views of the cliffs. Order tom yum goong (spicy shrimp soup) or a whole grilled fish. The night market in Krabi Town, the town for this stage of your trip, is also worth the trip for a more local evening—plan your return by road from Ao Nang; pad thai stalls, banana sweets and fresh fruit juices.

places.name: Lampang

visits.text: 20 km south of Lampang, Wat Phra That Lampang Luang sits on an artificial hillock surrounded by a 17th-century fortified wall—the Burmese used it as a stronghold. The Viharn Luang, built in 1476, is considered the oldest standing wooden building in Thailand. The interior pillars are decorated with lai kham, golden motifs on black lacquer. At the back of the viharn, the golden ku houses the Phra Chao Lan Thong Buddha, venerated since the 16th century.

In town, push through the door of Wat Phra Kaew Don Tao on the bank of the Wang River. This temple housed the Emerald Buddha for 32 years (1436-1468) before the statue departed for Chiang Mai and then Bangkok. What remains here is the Phra Kaew Don Tao Buddha in crystal, enshrined in a golden niche of the Mondop. The adjacent chedi dates from the 12th century.

activities.text: Ride in a horse-drawn carriage to tour the old town—the drivers know all the temples in the center. This is the only place in Thailand where this mode of transport is still in tourist operation.

visits.text: Loei is the most mountainous province in Isan. If you have the energy, leave early for Phu Kradueng, a basalt plateau reaching 1,325 meters. Allow for a round trip during the day from Loei to the trailhead, followed by an ascent on foot. The climb covers 5 to 9 km depending on the entry point. At the top is a 60 km² plateau with Scots pines, wildflowers and waterfalls. In the cool season (November-January), nighttime temperatures drop to 0°C.

A less strenuous alternative: Phu Ruea, about 59 km from Loei, a 50-minute drive. This national park in the mid-altitude mountains (1,365 m at the summit) offers short trails of 1 to 3 km with views over misty valleys. The sunset viewpoint is accessible by car.

activities.text: If you stay in the lowlands, explore Loei's central market in the morning. The province produces cotton and indigo: you'll find naturally dyed fabrics, bamboo baskets and fresh herbs you won't see in Bangkok markets. Vendors often come from surrounding villages starting at 5am.

visits.text: Phra Prang Sam Yot is a 13th-century Khmer temple - three prangs connected by a corridor, built during the reign of King Jayavarman VII. What distinguishes it: hundreds of crab-eating macaques have claimed it as their domain. They climb sculptures, leap from prang to prang, stare directly into your eyes. Stow all shiny objects - glasses, earrings - before entering. Don't stare too long at them. The temple's image appears on the Lopburi provincial flag.

Walk to King Narai's Palace - a vast 17th-century complex built by the sovereign who opened Thailand to European merchants. French, Dutch, and English ambassadors were received here. The national museum installed in the former royal granary displays Cham and Khmer sculptures, reconstructions of court life, and artifacts from local excavations.

activities.text: Get lost in Lopburi's alleyways. It's a city where monkeys have literally taken over: they run along electrical wires, enter grocery stores, jump on motorcycles. Locals have coexisted with them for generations. Watch local-macaque interactions - it's one of Thailand's most surreal spectacles.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Thailand: Bangkok, Ancient Kingdoms & the River Kwai

visits.text: A large lizard ambles across the lawn: at Lumphini Park, this is a common sight. The park is home to about 400 water monitors, lizards that can grow longer than 1.5 m and are harmless to humans. King Rama VI donated this land to the nation in 1925. The name comes from Lumbini, Nepal, the birthplace of the Buddha. Come in the late afternoon via Sala Daeng BTS station or Si Lom subway station. The park is open from 4:30 a.m. to 9 p.m.

activities.text: Rent a swan-shaped pedal boat on Lumphini Park’s artificial lake for 40 baht per half hour. The park covers 57.6 hectares, roughly the equivalent of 80 soccer fields. The statue of King Rama VI, erected in 1942 to celebrate the park’s creation, welcomes visitors at the entrance. In 2026, Sunday concerts were held from January 11 to March 1, starting at 5:30 p.m. Check the concert schedule for the year of your stay before planning an evening here.

places.name: Mae Hong Son

visits.text: Descending toward Mae Hong Son from Doi Inthanon, stop at the Doi Mae U Kho viewpoint if you're here between mid-November and mid-December. The hills are then covered with bua tong—wild yellow sunflowers that bloom on the slopes without being cultivated. Several kilometers of bright yellow against a green mountain backdrop. Outside this period, continue without stopping: the road itself is the spectacle.

Climb up to Wat Phra That Doi Kong Mu, perched on the hill overlooking the entire town. Two white Burmese stupas built in 1860 gleam at the summit. Below, Mae Hong Son bathes in a sea of morning mist. The spectacle is most striking at dawn.

Beside Nong Jong Kham Lake, the two sister temples—Wat Chong Kham (1827) and Wat Chong Klang (1867-71)—reflect their gilded tiered roofs in the water. They are temples in the Burmese Shan style, quite different from the Lanna wats seen elsewhere. Inside Wat Chong Klang, look for the paintings on glass depicting scenes from the Buddha's life.

activities.text: In the cool season (October-March), a small night market sets up along Nong Jong Kham Lake. Order khao tom - Thai evening rice soup - or try grilled river fish. The atmosphere feels more local than touristy.

places.name: Mukdahan

visits.text: Showing its age a little, Ho Kaeo Mukdahan Tower remains the city’s best observation point. Standing 65.5 m tall, it was built in 1996 to mark 50 years of King Rama IX’s reign. The second floor introduces the province’s eight ethnic groups. On the sixth floor, a terrace offers a full panoramic view of the Mekong and Laos. The tower is open from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; admission is 50 baht.

An 84 m white Buddha dominates the hill at Wat Roi Phra Phutthabat Phu Manorom, above Mukdahan. You can enter the statue, which has four levels leading up to the roof. A few minutes’ walk away, a green-and-blue naga, 122 m long, faces the Mekong. The viewpoint overlooks the city, the river, and Savannakhet in Laos. The site is open from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., with free admission. A pickup truck from the village takes visitors to the summit in exchange for a donation.

You can see the Second Thai–Lao Friendship Bridge from the riverbank in Mukdahan, near the shrine to the revered naga where residents come to pray. The bridge links Mukdahan with Savannakhet in Laos. It opened in December 2006, financed largely through a Japanese loan. Come in the late afternoon, when the heat eases along the riverbank.

activities.text: If you’re looking for an inexpensive sarong or lightweight pants, head to Mukdahan’s Indochina Market on the Mekong. It is one of the markets established to develop trade between Thailand and Laos. Pots and souvenirs are also sold here. Behind the stalls, a path follows the river, facing Savannakhet. The market is open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., but stay on the path for sunset.

places.name: Nakhon Phanom

visits.text: Modest but steeped in history, Ho Chi Minh’s house stands in the village of Ban Na Chok, 4 km from downtown Nakhon Phanom. The future leader of Vietnam lived here in exile in 1928 and 1929, among Vietnamese people who had settled in the region. The wooden stilt house, renovated in 2001, displays photographs and documents from that period. A memorial with a bronze statue stands in the same village. Admission is free. Come by taxi or bicycle, as no buses serve the site.

With yellow walls and a facade facing the Mekong, the Governor’s Residence Museum occupies a French colonial-style house built between 1912 and 1914. This style appears throughout the city, which faces former French Indochina. Inside, old photographs of Nakhon Phanom often have English captions. One bedroom remains furnished as it was for the visit of King Bhumibol and Queen Sirikit on November 12, 1955. The museum is open Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Wat Okat is a temple facing the Mekong, just steps from the Indochina Market. It houses two small seated Buddha statues, Phra Tiu and Phra Thiam, each about 60 cm tall. Local people believe their wooden originals date back to the 7th century. Every year, the statues are bathed during a ceremony on the full moon of the sixth lunar month, around May. Enter the sanctuary barefoot, with your shoulders and knees covered.

A Catholic church in a city of temples, St. Anne’s Church in Nong Saeng was built in 1926 on the banks of the Mekong. Its two towers are connected by a footbridge. Inside, light filters through colorful stained-glass windows. Avoid Mass times when visiting, or remain quietly at the back if a service is taking place.

activities.text: Walk along Nakhon Phanom’s Mekong promenade at sunrise, with Laos on the opposite bank. It forms part of the 70 km Sawan Chai Khong trail, which runs south to Wat Phra That Phanom. On the riverbank stands the statue of Phaya Si Sattanakharat, installed in 2016. It depicts a seven-headed naga. In local beliefs, the naga is a legendary serpent associated with the Mekong. On Friday through Sunday evenings, a pedestrian street beside the river turns into a market.

If you still have energy at the end of the day, watch the sunset from the river aboard the Mekong Paradise Cruise. According to the Bangkok Post in 2021, this restaurant boat departed every evening at around 5:30 p.m. for about 2 hours. The ticket covered the cruise, but food and drinks were extra. The departure point is near the Indochina Market and Wat Okat.

visits.text: Arrive in Nakhon Ratchasima, known as Korat. The statue of Thao Suranari has stood in the center of the old town since 1934. It depicts Mo, the wife of a local governor; she repelled the army of Vientiane in 1826 by arming women and prisoners. Thai people make pilgrimages here to bring her jasmine garlands and silk dresses.

Cross the moats that still mark the perimeter of the old fortified city. Several bastions have been restored. Maha Viravong National Museum, within a temple complex, displays Khmer sculptures from the region and prehistoric pottery from Isan excavations.

Step inside Wat Sala Loi, a modern temple whose ubosot is shaped like a Chinese junk resting on a pond. Built in 1973, it's unique in Thailand: the ship's bow and stern are carved with nagas, the windows shaped like portholes. A striking contrast with the Khmer temples visited in recent days.

activities.text: In the evening, head to Manat night market, steps from the Thao Suranari statue. It's one of the city's liveliest markets—pad kra pao (Thai basil stir-fry) cooked in a wok before your eyes, pork skewers marinated in turmeric, coconut milk desserts. A good stop for dinner before tomorrow's long drive to Chanthaburi.

places.name: Nan

visits.text: If you visit just one temple in Nan, choose Wat Phumin. Built in 1596, it has a cross-shaped layout. The building appears to rest on the backs of two nagas, legendary serpent guardians of water. Inside, four Buddha statues sit back-to-back, each facing a doorway. The murals were painted by local artist Nan Bua Phan during the restoration from 1867 to 1875. The most famous, Pu Man Ya Man, shows a man whispering into a woman’s ear. Admission is free from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.: come early to enjoy it in peace.

This palace, built in 1903 for Nan’s second-to-last prince, became the Nan National Museum in 1973. Its most remarkable object is a very dark brown elephant tusk measuring 97 cm long. It rests on a wooden stand shaped like Garuda, the giant bird of Hindu and Buddhist legends. The tusk is said to have been intended for a king of Nan about three centuries ago. Open Wednesday through Sunday, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., with admission costing 100 baht: don’t save it for a Monday.

Twenty-four sculpted elephants emerge halfway from the base of Wat Phra That Chang Kham, as if carrying the golden chedi on their backs. This chedi, a Buddhist monument housing a relic, dates to 1406. In the prayer hall, rebuilt in 1458, a large seated Buddha in the Lanna style, the art of the former northern kingdom, presides over the room. The temple faces the national museum: visit both on foot; admission is free.

People born in the Year of the Rabbit consider Wat Phra That Chae Haeng the temple of their zodiac sign. Founded in the 14th century east of the Nan River, it houses a gilded chedi about 55 m tall containing a relic of the Buddha. Two nagas with heads reaching about 4 m high flank the walkway. Free admission from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., 3 km from the center via Route 1168.

End the day at Wat Phra That Khao Noi, on a hill southwest of the city. A 9 m gilded Buddha in a standing, walking pose was erected here in 1999. The temple itself dates to 1487. Its viewpoint overlooks the city and mountains: this is the place in Nan to watch the sunset. Free admission, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: End the day at the night market next to Wat Phumin. It takes place just three evenings a week, Friday through Sunday, from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. This is a chance to see the temple again at dusk, then have dinner at the food stalls. If you arrive during the week, save this evening outing for your final stop in Nan.

places.name: Nong Khai

visits.text: Head to Sala Kaew Ku, 6 km east of town. This park of sculptures in unfinished concrete is the work of one man: Bunleua Sulilat, a Lao mystic exiled in 1975 during the communist revolution. He bought this land in 1978 and spent 20 years erecting over 100 giant statues, some 25 meters tall, funded solely by concrete donations from his followers. The Buddha seated on a seven-headed naga, the Wheel of Life you enter through a giant's mouth, the eight-armed goddesses—none were built by professionals. Sulilat died in 1996; his mummified body is visible under a glass bell jar on the third floor of the pavilion.

Visit Wat Pho Chai in central Nong Khai. It houses Luang Pho Phra Sai, a Lan Xang-style Buddha covered in gold, bronze and precious stones. According to legend, three similar Buddhas were crossing the Mekong on a raft: two sank, this one alone reached Nong Khai.

activities.text: Walk along the Mekong promenade in late afternoon. From the Thai side, you look directly at the hills of Laos 400 meters away. Fishermen cast their nets from small pirogues. The Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge, built in 1994, is visible to the east.

Browse Tha Sadet Market along the river, known for Lao products, medicinal herbs and indigo textiles. It's one of the few markets in the region where Thai and Lao traders still directly exchange their goods.

places.name: Pai

visits.text: Before leaving Mae Hong Son province, stop at the Su Tong Pae Bridge. This 500-meter bamboo bridge built in 2012 by monks and villagers crosses the rice paddies between Mae Hong Son and a neighboring monastery. Early in the morning, Buddhist novices cross it in single file to collect alms—a calm image, without any artifice.

Arrive in Pai and head straight to Pai Canyon, 5 km south of the village. Red-ochre rock formations with sharp ridges—the trails without guardrails run along crests sometimes barely a meter wide. Around 5pm, the sun grazes the walls and everything turns orange.

Rent a scooter and set out early for Mo Paeng Waterfall, 8 km from Pai. It consists of several natural pools with rocky slides. The water is soft and cool, the setting surrounded by jungle. It's noticeably quieter than the attractions in the village center.

On the way back, make a detour to the Land Split—a crack in the earth a few meters wide and a hundred meters long, opened suddenly during a landslide in 2008. It's surrounded by terraced rice paddies. Not essential, but it only takes ten minutes.

In late afternoon, climb up to Yun Lai viewpoint. The sun sets behind the Burmese ridges and the Pai valley fills with golden mist. It's also the best spot at sunrise—come at 5:30am if you're staying in the area.

activities.text: Pai's Walking Street comes alive every evening on the main street. Live musicians, pad thai stands, grilled sai ua sausages, fruit yogurt. Pai blends backpackers, hill tribe villagers, and Thai families—the atmosphere is warmer than cosmopolitan.

Plunge into the Tha Pai hot springs, 7 km from the center. A cold stream mixes with geothermal springs over rocks in the open air. In the cool season (November-February), it's particularly pleasant. Entry is paid.
