visits.text: If you get up early just once, make it for Pha Taem cliff. It overlooks the Mekong and Laos and faces east, with the sun rising directly ahead. The national park opens as early as 5 a.m. Around New Year’s, crowds gather along the cliff edge. Arrive before dawn with a flashlight.

You’ll then follow a walkway along the base of Pha Taem cliff to see its prehistoric paintings. They are 3,000–4,000 years old. The longest of the four groups stretches for about 180 m and contains more than 300 images in red ocher. They depict hands, animals, fish traps, and an enormous Mekong catfish, considered sacred in local beliefs. The cliff trail is about 4 km long. Allow 2 to 3 hours, and bring water and a hat.

At Sao Chaliang, sandstone pillars support stone caps wider than their bases, like giant mushrooms. The caps consist of harder rock than the bases. Wind and rain therefore wear away the bases faster, leaving the caps balanced on top. A 10-minute loop trail passes beneath the pillars. Admission is covered by the Pha Taem park ticket, which costs 200 baht per foreign adult.

activities.text: For a cool end to the morning, nothing beats Thung Na Mueang Waterfall in Pha Taem park, near the Mekong. Its flow depends on rainfall: favor the rainy season and the beginning of the cool season; it may run dry during the dry season. The site is open from 7 a.m. to 4 p.m., with no additional ticket required. It makes a pleasant break after the paintings, before heading back down to spend the night in Khong Chiam.

days_plan.itin_title: Mekong Isan in 8 Days: That Phanom, Pha Taem, and Ubon

visits.text: “Phae” means a sparse forest, and “mueang phi” evokes a silent, almost haunted place: Phae Mueang Phi lives up to its name. Across roughly 80 hectares, rain and wind have sculpted earthen pillars, cliffs, and mushroom-shaped rocks. You can explore the park without a real hike, from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.: arrive in the morning, before the heat sets in.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Lanna in 7 Days: Nan, Bo Kluea, Phrae, Phayao

visits.text: It took 33 years to build the great Buddha at Wat Si Khom Kham, begun in 1491 and completed in 1524. Known as Phra Chao Ton Luang, this seated Buddha of brick and gilded stucco measures about 14 m from knee to knee. Its height varies by source, from 16 to 18.5 m. It is the province’s most revered Buddha image. The temple stands beside Kwan Phayao Lake and is open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.: visit before your lakeside walk.

Ho Watanatham Nithat, Phayao’s cultural exhibition hall, helps you understand the city before a lakeside walk. Displays include historical objects, documents, old photographs, and accounts of local history. Phayao was once a city-state, founded nine to ten centuries ago. The hall is about 1 km from Wat Si Khom Kham: allow 45 minutes.

At sunset, the waters of Kwan Phayao turn orange beside the city. This lake covers about 20 km² but is only about 1.5 m deep. It occupies a natural basin. Its water level rose after 1941, when a sluice gate, a kind of small dam, was completed on the Ing River. Around 50 species of fish live here. Rent a bike to follow the bike paths along the shore, lined with restaurants.

If the sky is clear, head up to Wat Analayo Thipphayaram, a temple perched on the slopes of Doi Busarakham, the hill overlooking Phayao. Plan a round trip by car from Phayao for this visit. Its terraces offer views of the city and Kwan Phayao Lake. Morning is best, when the air is cooler and the light is clearer for photos.

activities.text: Take a boat to Wat Tilok Aram, an ancient temple in the middle of Kwan Phayao. This temple was submerged when the lake’s sluice gate raised the water level in the early 1940s. Today, it is accessible only by boat. Go in the morning or late afternoon: the midday sun is intense on the water.

For us, the highlight of Phayao is an evening stroll along its pedestrian street, known as the walking street. You can eat local food and buy souvenirs made by communities in the province. It is an easy way to have dinner after a day by the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Lanna in 7 Days: Nan, Bo Kluea, Phrae, Phayao

visits.text: Start with Tham Khao Luang Cave, 2.5 miles north of town. Descend rock steps: a 98-foot-high chamber opens before you. Two openings in the pierced vault drop columns of natural light directly onto the 170 Buddha statues populating the 3 chambers. Rama V himself came here to meditate as a young monk. The morning light show is the most powerful.

Next, climb to Phra Nakhon Khiri Historical Park - the summer palace of King Mongkut (Rama IV), completed in 1860 on a 302-foot hill overlooking the city. A funicular provides summit access (40 baht round-trip). On three successive crests: the white chedi of Phra That Chom Phet, the former royal apartments transformed into a museum, and the royal Wat Phra Kaeo. Panoramic 360° view across the Phetchaburi plain.

activities.text: Phetchaburi is famous for its khanom - traditional Thai desserts. As you stroll through the old town, look out for the shops selling coconut and palm sugar sweets. The evening market starts around 5 PM on Phanitchatham Road.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Thailand: Bangkok, Ancient Kingdoms & the River Kwai

places.name: Phimai

visits.text: Enter the Prasat Hin Phimai complex by crossing the Naga bridge, whose railings carved in the shape of seven-headed serpents symbolically carry you from the human world to the realm of the gods. This 11th-century Khmer temple was built BEFORE Angkor Wat—some historians believe the central white sandstone prang directly inspired Angkor's architects. Its distinctive feature: unlike most Hindu Khmer temples, Phimai has always been Buddhist. The rectangular enclosure measures 1,020 by 580 meters—comparable to Angkor Wat.

750 meters north of the ruins, Phimai National Museum displays a statue of Jayavarman VII, the great 12th-century Khmer king, and numerous carved lintels from the excavations. One of the finest Khmer museums outside Cambodia.

Walk around Sai Ngam, Thailand's largest banyan tree. Its aerial roots have spread over an area of about 2,500 m² along the Mun River. The mass of intertwined trunks creates a dense forest on its own. Thais attribute spiritual powers to it and hang makeshift offerings on it.

activities.text: Stroll through the streets of Phimai's old town on foot. Pratu Chai gate, a few hundred meters south of the temple, is one of the vestiges of the ancient fortified city - it once guarded the royal road to Angkor, 225 km southeast. Phimai sees few foreign tourists: enjoy the tranquil atmosphere of the evening market to sample Isan specialties - gai yang (chicken grilled with herbs), sticky rice, and som tam pounded in a mortar to order.

places.name: Phrae

visits.text: Khum Chao Luang, the residence of Phrae’s last reigning prince, has 72 doors and windows framed in carved wood. Built in 1892, this two-story brick building blends European style with that of Lanna, the former northern kingdom. The palace was also used to administer justice. At its center, a room with no light held prisoners considered the most dangerous. Admission is free from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; allow at least 1 hour.

The pale pink Vongburi House features finely cut teak decorations on its gables, balconies, and windows. It was built in 1907 for a princely family from Phrae by carpenters from Guangdong, China, assisted by local craftspeople. Inside, antique furniture, silverware, and family papers tell the story of the teak trade era. Those papers include bills of sale for enslaved people. Admission costs 30 baht; posted hours are 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Saturday.

Make your way around Phrae’s city walls, which stand about 7 m high and encircle the old town for nearly 4 km. A moat about twenty meters wide runs along their base. The walls are said to date back more than eleven centuries. Follow them by bike or on foot late in the day, when the heat eases.

In our view, Wat Chom Sawan is Phrae’s most evocative temple, built in the Burmese style. Its buildings are made almost entirely of teak, the wood that made the city’s fortune. It stands about 1 km from the provincial government headquarters. Visit in the morning, before the heat sets in, then head to Khum Chao Luang.

It looks centuries old, yet Ban Prathapjai House was only built between 1972 and 1976. Its owner brought together 130 teak pillars, made from trunks said to be about three centuries old. Rounding the number down, it is known as the “house of a hundred pillars.” Visit after Vongburi House: the two showcase Phrae’s teak in two very different eras.

A piece of satin fabric gave Wat Phra That Cho Hae its name. According to tradition, it once wrapped the relic kept in the chedi, a hair of the Buddha. This 33 m octagonal chedi, covered in gilded copper plates, crowns a hill about ten kilometers southeast of Phrae. Around 120 steps lined with nagas lead from the parking lot up to the temple grounds. Admission is free: come late in the afternoon, when the copper catches the light.

activities.text: Follow Route 101 toward Nan for 4 km to reach Thung Hong, the village of mo hom. This cotton, dyed a deep indigo blue using a local plant called hom, has become one of Phrae’s symbols. Shops selling shirts, scarves, and bags line both sides of the road. Not every item is hand-dyed: ask before buying.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Lanna in 7 Days: Nan, Bo Kluea, Phrae, Phayao

map_keywords: Wat Phra That Cho Hae Phrae

visits.text: Route 1148 has 134 curves over 118 km, and Phu Langka is its highlight. Stop at the roadside Pha Chang Noi viewpoint to see the limestone valley below. The massif rises to about 1,720 m. The sea of clouds, a blanket of mist filling the valleys, is most often visible at sunrise. At midday, a brief stop is enough.

activities.text: Park at Phu Langka Forest Park, where a regular car can reach the nature discovery area. Trails lead from there for observing the forest and its birds. Doi Phu Lom, a nearby peak at about 1,600 m, offers a 360-degree view. Some very steep upper tracks require a 4x4.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Lanna in 7 Days: Nan, Bo Kluea, Phrae, Phayao

visits.text: Head out early for Phu Pha Thoep National Park, 17 km south of Mukdahan: it opens around 7:30 a.m., and the bare rock heats up quickly. The trail through the Hin Thoep rock group crosses a field of mushroom-shaped sandstone formations. Their silhouettes resemble swans, crowns, camels, or crocodiles. Higher up, a viewpoint overlooks Mukdahan, the Mekong, and Laos. Trail markings among the rocks are confusing: follow the signs and bring water.

Fa Mue Daeng Cave, the Cave of Red Hands, preserves around ten handprints painted in red ocher. They were made using a stencil technique: people placed a hand against the rock and sprayed pigment around it. Archaeologists date them to 3,000–5,000 years ago. Reaching the cave requires a hike through the park: ask the staff about the trail before setting out, rather than planning it as a short detour from the Hin Thoep rocks. Look without touching the rock wall.

days_plan.itin_title: Mekong Isan in 8 Days: That Phanom, Pha Taem, and Ubon

places.name: Phuket

visits.text: Get lost in Phuket's old town, around Thalang Road and Soi Romanee. The Sino-Portuguese shophouses with pastel facades date from the early 20th-century mining boom, when Hokkien merchants and Portuguese engineers fused their styles. Soi Romanee was once Phuket's entertainment street—today, its pink houses house cafés and boutiques. It's the most photographed street on the island.

Step into the Thai Hua Museum on Krabi Road, housed in a former Sino-Portuguese school from 1934. The exhibition traces the history of Phuket's Baba-Nyonya (Peranakan) community—which emerged from unions between Hokkien Chinese miners and local Thai women, with its own cuisine, language, and crafts.

On Sundays from 4 p.m. to 10 p.m., Thalang Road transforms into a pedestrian market. Street food stalls, local musicians, and artisans take over the street: it's the best time to sample Phuket's Sino-Thai specialties in the open air.

Reach Phang Nga Bay by longtail from Tha Dan Pier, approximately 86 km from Phuket, a 1-hour-25-minute drive before the boat trip. First stop: Koh Tapu, a 20-meter rock rising vertically from the sea - famous as 'James Bond Island' since the filming of 'The Man with the Golden Gun' in 1974. The actual name of the neighboring island, Khao Phing Kan, means 'mountains leaning against each other' - an enormous split limestone block rests against its twin.

Stop at Koh Panyee, a floating village founded by Muslim fishermen over 200 years ago. All the houses, the school, the mosque, and even a soccer field are perched on stilts against a vertical limestone tower. Stroll along the wooden walkways—away from the main flow of tourists, a few alleys still offer glimpses of the village's daily life.

activities.text: Drive from Khao Lak to Phuket (1.5 hours). Stay in the old town rather than Patong—you'll sleep in a listed building, 10 minutes' walk from everything that matters.

Go hunting for the street art scattered around the old town since 2014, when Phuket and Georgetown (Penang) became sister cities. Look for Alex Face's work on Phang Nga Road and Rukkij Kuanhavej's murals at the corner of Soi Romanee.

Full-day longtail excursion in Phang Nga Bay. Depart from Tha Dan Pier (Phang Nga Town), approximately 86 km from Phuket, a 1-hour-25-minute drive before the boat trip - the boat journey is shorter and you encounter fewer speedboats. Choose a private longtail for more flexibility.
Kayaking in the 'hongs' - sea caves carved into limestone cliffs by erosion. Inside, a miniature jungle and a secret lagoon await you. Operators based in Phang Nga provide guides who paddle for you.

visits.text: Three overlapping wood-shingle roofs crown Wat Ton Laeng, descending almost to its walls. This roughly 200-year-old temple is built in the Tai Lue style, named after a Tai-speaking people with a strong presence in the Pua Valley. It stands on a peninsula between the Pua and Khwang Rivers. The hall is sometimes closed for lack of visitors: the roof alone makes the detour worthwhile.

The best view of the Pua Valley is from Wat Phuket, a modern temple about 3 km east of town. It also houses a school for young monks. Head up in the late afternoon, when the low-angle light brings out the rice fields and farms on the valley floor.

activities.text: Walk among the rice fields of Ban Sila Laeng and Silaphet, two villages in the Pua Valley 7 km apart. From September to November, the fields turn from vivid green to harvest gold. Stay on the paddy dikes, the low earthen banks separating the fields, and ask before entering a cultivated plot.

Ban Hia, near Pua, keeps traditional Tai Lue weaving alive at the Phaeo Phafai workshop. This is the place to see how the fabrics sold in the valley are made. In central Pua, other shops sell textiles from the Lue and the Hmong, a mountain people: compare before buying.

If the heat builds, head to Sila Phet Waterfall in Ban Pa Tong, in Pua District. The water cascades down several tiers, and you can swim here. Bring sandals that stay securely on your feet on wet rocks.

visits.text: Soak your feet at the Raksawarin hot springs, 2 km from central Ranong. The water constantly emerges at 65°C. King Rama V visited in 1890 and named the access road 'Chon Ra-u', meaning 'hot water'. The public pools are free; private areas are available for a small fee.

Stroll along Saphan Pla fishing port, one of the busiest along the Andaman coast. Across the Kraburi River, you can see Kawthaung — Myanmar's southernmost continental point — just a few hundred meters away. Colorful longboats shuttle between the two countries.

activities.text: Coastal drive from Chumphon to Ranong (around 2 hours) via Highway 4, which follows a mountainous, heavily forested shoreline. Ranong is Thailand's rainiest province—8 months of rainy season—but this gives it remarkably dense vegetation.

In the evening, stroll through the night market on Kamlangsap Road, 200 m from Highway 4. Small but lively, it brings together the region's Thai-Burmese specialties—with a strong Hokkien influence in the snacks and soups.

visits.text: In 1975, That Phanom’s great stupa collapsed. Its replica at Wat Phra That Renu shows what it looked like. A stupa is a spire-shaped Buddhist monument that houses relics. This one was erected in 1918 as a smaller version of That Phanom’s: about 35 m tall, white and gold. Admission is free during the day. Allow 45 minutes before continuing to That Phanom, 15 km to the south.

activities.text: You can buy Phu Thai textiles right on the grounds of Wat Phra That Renu. This community in Renu Nakhon is known for its handwoven silk and cotton. On Saturday evenings, a market sets up around the temple. You’ll find indigo-dyed fabrics, matmi (fabric whose threads are dyed before weaving), and embroidered clothing. During the week, walk through the village to see the looms.

visits.text: Three thousand holes: that is the meaning of Sam Phan Bok, a name combining the Thai word for three thousand and the Lao word for holes. This reddish sandstone plateau in the Mekong’s riverbed is riddled with round hollows. The river’s swirling currents carved them over the centuries. It emerges only during the dry season, roughly from December to May. For the rest of the year, it is almost entirely underwater. Come at sunrise or sunset, wearing shoes with good traction.

activities.text: The best overall view of Sam Phan Bok is from the river. Long-tail boats—narrow boats whose engines drive propellers at the end of long shafts—depart from Hat Salueng Beach. The trip lasts about 1 hour and covers 4 km along the rocks. Trips are still possible when part of the plateau is underwater. Expect to pay around 1,000 baht per boat, which can be split among several people.

visits.text: You might think you were in a canyon in the American West, yet Sao Din Na Noi lies 60 km south of Nan. These earth pillars, known to locals as Hom Chom, were formed by erosion from water and wind. The softer layers were swept away, while the harder ones remained standing. Come early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light accentuates their contours.

activities.text: Continue walking to Kok Suea, the “tiger enclosure,” where earthen walls form a natural enclosure. Allow 1 to 2 hours for the entire site, which is open from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. It is part of Si Nan National Park: admission costs 100 baht for foreign visitors and also covers Doi Samer Dao.

visits.text: Long drive south from Pai. Arrive in Sukhothai in late afternoon and enter the historical park directly—it's open until 6pm. This is where the first independent Thai kingdom was founded in 1238, breaking free from the Khmer empire. Its king Ramkhamhaeng invented the Thai alphabet here in 1292. Start with Wat Mahathat, when the light turns low.

Wat Sa Si, a few hundred meters away, sits on a small island connected by a footbridge. A Sri Lankan-style chedi and a standing brick Buddha reflect in the water lilies. This is one of the most photographed spots in the park, especially at sunset.

Leave early for Wat Si Chum, in the northern zone. Approach the narrow slit in the brick mondop's facade: the Phra Achana Buddha—“the one who knows no fear”—stares at you from 15 meters high. Its fingers alone measure 1.3 meters. This is the largest seated stone Buddha in the park. An inscription found here in 1293 is the oldest written document in the Thai alphabet.

Return to the central zone for Wat Si Sawai. Its three Khmer-style prangs—square-based towers—date from the 12th century, even before the kingdom's founding. This was a Hindu sanctuary dedicated to Shiva, transformed into a Buddhist temple during the expansion of Theravada Buddhism.

The Ramkhamhaeng National Museum, just at the entrance to the central zone, displays the 1292 stele with the first Thai alphabet inscriptions, bronze Sukhothai-style Buddhas, and Sawankhalok ceramics. Allow 1.5 hours to tour it properly.

The northern zone also houses Wat Phra Phai Luang—three 12th-century Khmer prangs surrounded by moats. The site is overgrown with vegetation in places and practically deserted most of the time. A very different atmosphere from the restored central zone.

If you have half a day to spare, push on to Si Satchanalai, 50 km north. This was Sukhothai's twin city—just as large, just as well preserved, with ten times fewer visitors. Wat Chang Lom there is surrounded by sculpted elephants in the round. The atmosphere is that of a forgotten archaeological site.

activities.text: Rent a bicycle at the park entrance—30 to 50 baht per day. The terrain is flat and the paths are paved. It's the most pleasant way to move between the different zones of the site.

Cycle to the temples in the western zone, less visited. Wat Saphan Hin is built on a 200-meter hill—a long stone pathway leads to a tall standing Buddha overlooking the surrounding rice paddies. Practically no one after 4pm.

Before leaving Sukhothai, buy Sawankhalok ceramics at the old town market. These blue-gray celadon-style pottery pieces, manufactured in the region since the 13th century, are the oldest Thai craft objects.

visits.text: Talat Noi, Thai for “little market,” is an old Chinese neighborhood along the river, on the edge of Chinatown. Chinese families settled here shortly after Bangkok was founded. Portuguese settlers from Ayutthaya, the former capital, built a church here as early as 1786: the current Holy Rosary Church, in the Gothic Revival style, dates from the late 19th century. In the alleys, workshops weld and restore old car parts near walls covered with murals. Stop by the courtyard of So Heng Tai House, a 19th-century Chinese residence that is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: The best excuse to linger in Talat Noi comes on a plate: kuaitiao khua kai, stir-fried rice noodles with chicken. The dish originated during World War II as an adaptation of chicken rice porridge. After your meal, have a coffee in one of the old Chinese houses or a former waterfront warehouse: some of these buildings are more than 200 years old. Avoid Mondays, when several neighborhood establishments are closed.

visits.text: Gold leaf, lotus buds, and monks’ chants: at Wat Phra That Phanom, the great golden stupa rises more than 50 m. It is the province’s main Buddhist shrine. According to tradition, it holds a chest bone of the Buddha. On August 11, 1975, after several days of heavy rain, the tower collapsed. It was rebuilt and reopened in 1979. A small museum displays photographs of the collapse. Come at dawn, between 5 a.m. and 7 a.m., when the monks make their rounds to receive food offerings. Cover your shoulders and knees.

Wat Hua Wiang marks the northern end of That Phanom’s riverfront. The temple’s age is unknown. Its ordination hall, where novices become monks, was built between 1917 and 1921. Its interior walls are painted. Stop by as you follow the Mekong, before or after visiting Wat Phra That Phanom. Admission is free; wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.

activities.text: Walk down from Wat Phra That Phanom toward That Phanom’s riverfront, passing beneath a kind of triumphal arch set in the middle of a traffic circle. Between the arch and the river, old shophouses, often weathered, preserve the feel of the town as it once was. Along the riverbank, a promenade runs past restaurants serving freshwater fish. Laos is directly across the river. The whole town is walkable.

Small town, wide choice of street food: That Phanom’s night market sets up every evening north of the temple. Stalls line the road running alongside the large ponds. Among the offerings are fried frogs. It’s the easiest option for dinner in That Phanom.

places.name: Trang

visits.text: Take a detour to Tham Le Khao Kob Cave, 35 km north of Trang. You visit it by rowboat on an underground river that runs through a limestone massif. The boatmen know every centimeter of the vaulted ceiling—in certain passages, you have to lie down in the boat to avoid touching it. Locals call the narrowest section “the dragon's backbone”.

In the evening, explore Trang's night market, known as 'Centrepoint,' a few streets east of the train station. Trang is renowned for its dim sum and charcoal-roasted pork — a legacy of Hokkien immigrants who populated the town when the tin mines were running full tilt. Vendors offer 20 varieties of curry at once. Order by pointing.

activities.text: Return ferry to the mainland from Koh Lanta (1.5–2 hours via Trang or Pak Meng pier). From the pier, drive to Trang (30–45 min). Trang is an ordinary Thai town with extraordinary cuisine.

Roti mataba for breakfast at one of the halal stalls near the station: pancake stuffed with spiced beef, onion, and egg, served with yellow curry for dipping. It's Trang's morning specialty that everyone orders standing up before heading out.

visits.text: Wat Thung Si Muang, a wooden temple dating to the reign of Rama III (1824–1851), keeps its most unusual feature in the middle of a pond. This is the ho trai, the library of sacred texts, built on stilts. The water kept away termites and insects that ate the palm-leaf manuscripts. The temple was originally built to house a copy of the Buddha’s footprint. It is open from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, and admission is free.

Every July, beeswax sculptures from the Candle Festival are displayed in Thung Si Muang Park in central Ubon. During the rest of the year, you can see a golden column shaped like a royal barge, decorated with garudas, birds from Hindu and Buddhist legends, and nagas. A more modest monument was erected by former Allied prisoners of war to thank the residents who helped them during World War II. The park is just north of the national museum: visit both on foot.

If you are in Ubon between Wednesday and Sunday, set aside 1 hour 30 minutes for the Ubon Ratchathani National Museum. It occupies the former city hall, a yellow building dating to 1918 that became a museum in 1989. Exhibits include pottery from Isan dating back about 3,000 years and rare Buddha statues. The museum is open from 9 AM to 4 PM. Admission cost 100 baht in 2025.

Next, visit Wat Si Ubon Rattanaram, which the city regards as its founding temple. The grand Candle Festival parade sets off from here in July, at the start of the retreat monks observe during the rainy season. That morning, more than fifty floats carry beeswax sculptures through the city. Remove your shoes before entering the halls.

A piece of India in the heart of Isan: Wat Phra That Nong Bua takes its shape from the Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment. Its 56 m white-and-gold stupa was built in 1956 to mark 2,500 years of Buddhism. Inside, golden pillars rise to the top around a seated Buddha. The temple is open from 6:30 AM to 8 PM, and admission is free. Save it for the end of the day.

Beneath the trees, silence: Wat Nong Pah Pong is a forest monastery on the outskirts of Ubon. It was founded by Ajahn Chah (1918–1992), a Thai meditation master. A three-story museum tells the story of his life. The monastery also hosts retreats in vipassana, a form of meditation based on self-observation. It is open from 5 AM to 6 PM, and admission is free. Come dressed in clothing that covers your body.

Wat Pah Nanachat was founded in 1975 by Ajahn Chah in the village of Bung Wai, 15 km from Ubon. It is a monastery for foreigners who want to follow the Thai forest monk tradition. Teaching is in English. Visitors are welcome. To stay there, write well in advance, as places are limited. A meal is offered to the monks every morning at 8 AM: plan your visit for afterward.

activities.text: Start the day with a bowl of kuay chap yuan at Ubon Ocha, a well-known spot in Ubon. This Thai-Vietnamese noodle soup comes with pork, chicken, or Vietnamese sausage. The restaurant also serves eggs cooked in a small skillet and Vietnamese-style bread. It is open from 5:30 AM to 3 PM. Arrive early, before heading to the forest monasteries.

Huk Mun Market, on the banks of the Mun River, is worth a visit on your last evening. Makeshift bars and restaurants set up here, some in old train cars. Concerts liven up the evening. The market is open from 4 PM to midnight, but it gets busiest after 6 PM. Sample small portions of several dishes as you move from stall to stall.

places.name: Udon Thani

visits.text: Drive 50 km east of Udon Thani to Ban Chiang, a UNESCO archaeological site since 1992. An American Harvard student tripped over a root here in 1966 - and discovered pottery dating to 1,500 BC. Excavations have uncovered hundreds of burials, bronze tools, copper jewelry and the red spiral pottery on an orange background that has become Udon Thani's symbol.

At Wat Pho Si Nai temple, 500 meters from the museum, visit the display of the Ban Chiang excavations. Reconstructed burials show the arrangement of pottery and bones in the soil as it appeared when they were discovered. The site helps you understand the work of archaeologists.

If you're here between mid-December and late February: visit the Red Lotus Sea (Talay Bua Daeng) on Nong Han Lake, 45 minutes from Udon Thani. Thousands of pink lotuses cover several hectares of the lake at dawn. Take a boat early in the morning - the flowers close after 10am. Off-season: replace with a visit to Phu Phra Bat Historical Park (Dvaravati-era carved rocks, 65 km away).

activities.text: In the evening, wander Udon Thani's walking street in the city center. Isan cuisine expresses itself here in its most direct form: som tam Isan (shredded papaya, cherry tomatoes, chili and fermented crab paste - sharper and saltier than the Bangkok version), charcoal-grilled gai yang, sticky rice compressed in a small bamboo basket.

visits.text: The colorful fragments covering Wat Arun’s main tower are pieces of Chinese porcelain and seashells. This porcelain arrived from China as ballast, meaning weight placed at the bottom of ships to stabilize them. The builders therefore obtained it cheaply. The name means “Temple of Dawn,” in honor of Aruna, a Hindu deity associated with the rising sun. Admission costs 200 baht, and opening hours are 8 AM to 6 PM. Have your canal boat drop you off here; otherwise, a ferry crosses the river from Tha Tien Pier.

visits.text: The highlight of Wat Pho awaits at the end of the main hall, before the feet of the Reclining Buddha. The statue measures 46 m long and 15 m tall. Each 4.5 m-long sole is inlaid with mother-of-pearl in 108 panels depicting auspicious symbols. The temple also has more than a thousand Buddha statues and four large 42 m chedis, reliquary towers dedicated to the first four kings of the current dynasty. Admission is 300 baht, and it opens at 8 AM. Remove your shoes before entering the halls.

activities.text: Give your legs a break before you start walking again: Wat Pho houses a school of traditional Thai medicine and massage. It moved into the temple in the 1950s. Its practitioners offer visitors Thai massages or foot massages lasting from 30 minutes to 2 hours. Thirty minutes is enough to recover from a morning spent on your feet at the Grand Palace. The service operates from 8 AM to 7:30 PM, and both types of massage cost the same.

visits.text: Climb the 344 steps of the Golden Mount, the hill rising above Wat Saket, crowned with a golden chedi (reliquary tower). It came into being after a failure. Under King Rama III, a large chedi collapsed during construction because Bangkok’s soft soil could not support its weight. A small chedi was later built on the mound and covered in gold. Along the climb, visitors ring rows of bells. Admission for the climb is 100 baht, from 7 AM to 7 PM: come early, before the heat, for views across the entire city.

activities.text: The river breeze feels good after the climb up the Golden Mount. Take a taxi to Tha Chang Pier, then board a Chao Phraya express boat heading south. Orange-flag boats run only Monday through Friday: on weekends, ask at the pier about available services. These public boats provide everyday transportation for local residents. Along the way, you pass Wat Arun and travel under Memorial Bridge. Get off at Marine Department Pier (N4), the most convenient stop for Talat Noi. Tickets cost 10 to 32 baht depending on the distance.

visits.text: In 1955, ropes snapped, and Wat Traimit discovered its treasure. Workers were moving a large Buddha statue covered in plaster. It fell, revealing gold beneath the broken pieces. This gold Buddha stands 3 m tall and weighs 5.5 tonnes. At some unknown date, it had been coated in plaster to prevent theft. Admission costs 100 baht, with opening hours from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Another floor of the building tells the story of Chinatown and its Chinese immigrants.

visits.text: Yaowarat, Chinatown’s main street, winds for about 1.5 km. According to tradition, its curved route resembles a dragon’s body, a sign of good luck for business. The street was built between 1892 and 1900. It is nicknamed the “gold road” for its many gold shops. Come during the day for the jewelry stores, then take a break during the hottest hours before dinner. By subway, get off at Wat Mangkon station and take exit 1.

activities.text: If you have just one street food meal in Bangkok, make it on Yaowarat. After dark, the street becomes one big “dining street,” drawing people from across the city. Food carts start setting up at 5 p.m., and crowds peak between 6:30 p.m. and 10:30 p.m. At the most popular stalls, expect a wait of 20 to 40 minutes: one person holds the table while the other orders. Bring cash in small bills, as few vendors accept cards. Some take Mondays off.
